lessons.title: Send transactional email with Resend
lessons.concept: Email is asynchronous delivery: accepting a request, handing the message to a provider, and observing delivery are three different events. In “Send transactional email with Resend”, the concrete input is an order receipt triggered server-side after a paid transition and correlated with an internal identifier. transactional email means: A message triggered by a specific recipient action, such as an order or password reset. The model is complete only when you trigger from confirmed server state, validate recipient and reference, then store an idempotent send key and can observe that Resend accepts a message containing the expected reference, the server retains its provider identifier, and no key reaches the browser.

explanation.title: Simple analogy
explanation.text: Sending email is like posting a parcel: the counter receipt proves acceptance, not that the recipient opened the parcel. Here the part you will actually inspect is a minimal server function that sends an order receipt without exposing the API key; stop using the analogy if it obscures the technical boundary shown by the code.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: Start by bounding this lesson’s case: an order receipt triggered server-side after a paid transition and correlated with an internal identifier. Keep the Resend key server-side, separate message construction from delivery, and record the provider identifier for delivery diagnosis. The term transactional email is not a decorative label: A message triggered by a specific recipient action, such as an order or password reset. It determines what enters, which authority may act, and which observation counts as evidence rather than an impression.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: In exercises/21-email/resend-order.ts, the example deliberately reduces the system to a minimal server function that sends an order receipt without exposing the API key. Read each line as one responsibility, then run npm run build. The main failure to trigger is: checkout sends mail directly before payment confirmation and a reload creates two receipts. It shows why the professional correction is to trigger from confirmed server state, validate recipient and reference, then store an idempotent send key, not to conceal the error.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: In a real system, the happy path is only one case among retries, invalid input, and partial outages. The expected proof is that Resend accepts a message containing the expected reference, the server retains its provider identifier, and no key reaches the browser. Apply the same evidence to order confirmations, contact requests, and support-inbox processing, using a correlation trace without secrets or personal data so both success and failure remain explainable.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: Start by bounding this lesson’s case: a small public form that hands a message to EmailJS without confusing a public key with a server secret. The model is complete only when you reserve EmailJS for low-sensitivity mail, bound and encode fields, restrict origins, and add rate limiting or an anti-abuse challenge and can observe that the browser sends only expected fields with the public identifier, while domain, template, and anti-abuse limits reject an unauthorized origin.
teaching.why: Start by bounding this lesson’s case: a small public form that hands a message to EmailJS without confusing a public key with a server secret. Understand that a public key is visible, validate and limit in the UI, then strengthen the design with quotas, provider templates, and abuse protection. The term public key is not a decorative label: An identifier designed for distribution to clients that never replaces server authentication. It determines what enters, which authority may act, and which observation counts as evidence rather than an impression.

teaching.how:
In exercises/21-email/emailjs-contact.ts, the example deliberately reduces the system to a typed form submission that rejects short messages and embeds no private secret. Read each line as one responsibility, then run npm run build. The main failure to trigger is: the form is assumed safe because the key is called publicKey, then bots exhaust the quota. It shows why the professional correction is to reserve EmailJS for low-sensitivity mail, bound and encode fields, restrict origins, and add rate limiting or an anti-abuse challenge, not to conceal the error.
In a real system, the happy path is only one case among retries, invalid input, and partial outages. The expected proof is that the browser sends only expected fields with the public identifier, while domain, template, and anti-abuse limits reject an unauthorized origin. Apply the same evidence to order confirmations, contact requests, and support-inbox processing, using a correlation trace without secrets or personal data so both success and failure remain explainable.
